extracted.intended_audience: scholars, natural philosophers, educators, clergy, and learned readers interested in reforming learning and scholarship
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative guidance for diagnosing the 'diseases' of learning and for improving scholarship: identifies vices (scholastic disputation, imposture, credulity, misplaced ends) and prescribes habits (universality of reading, observation, independent judgment, union of theory and practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic subtleties and contentious disputation
rubrics_metrics.description: When inquiry descends into endless distinctions and decisions it ends in 'monstrous altercations and barking questions' and brings popular contempt upon knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let inquiry become a fruitless wrangling of subtleties; prefer usefulness and benefit to human life over mere verbal contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice variety and universality of reading and contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of a wide variety and universality of reading and contemplation would have made scholastics 'excellent lights' and advanced learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine broad reading and contemplation rather than isolating within a narrow received authority; diversity of sources strengthens judgment and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abandon primary sources and observation for pride or received authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride inclined schoolmen to leave the oracle of God’s word and, in natural inquiry, the oracle of God’s works, adoring the images of their own minds or a few received authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep to primary sources—scripture and nature—and avoid substituting personal inventions or limited authorities for direct observation and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposture and credulity (delight in deceiving and aptness to be deceived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceit or untruth destroys the essential form of knowledge; imposture and credulity often concur and corrupt reputation for truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against both deliberate falsification and facile belief; note the affinity between fiction and belief ('Fingunt simul creduntque') and check reports carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of facile credit: history/matter-of-fact vs art/opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility of credit takes two forms: belief of history (matters of fact) and belief of arts/opinions, each requiring different scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize historical/reported miracles, relics and the like especially strictly; treat matters of art/opinion with appropriate critical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep manifest truth distinct from fabulous or prodigious narrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle is praised for mingling manifest truth sparingly with feigned matter and for casting prodigious narrations into a separate book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weaken reliable observational material by mixing it with doubtful or fabulous reports; record rarities separately so they do not corrupt rules and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of speculative sciences that veil error with enigma and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences like astrology, natural magic, and alchemy have noble pretences but their theories and practices are 'full of error and vanity' and often veiled by enigmatical writings and oral traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand experimental verification and transparency; recognize that some speculative pursuits (e.g., alchemy) nonetheless produced useful experiments, but avoid being misled by obscure style or secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating authors as dictators; cultivate independent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Overmuch credit to authors, making their words absolute, has kept sciences low in growth; disciples should temporarily believe but ultimately judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Couple required deference in early learning ('Oportet discentem credere') with later independent evaluation ('Oportet edoctum judicare'); encourage critical reexamination over perpetual captivity to authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme preference for either antiquity or novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Affecting the extremes—adoration of antiquity or of novelty—distorts judgement; antiquity deserves reverence but discovery should lead to progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect useful antiquity but allow and pursue new additions where warranted; seek the right path by weighing ancient ways and advancing from them when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to new discoveries; do not distrust present capacity for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Error arises from doubting that anything new can now be found; history (e.g., Alexander, Columbus) shows great enterprises at first thought impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a priori refusal of new claims; investigate plausibly novel proposals rather than dismissing them because they appear unprecedented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume that past rejection implies worthlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceit that the best of former opinions has always prevailed leads men to avoid new searches; time often carries off the weighty while passing down the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamine neglected or rejected ideas on their merits rather than assuming their prior rejection settles their worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay premature formalization into exact methods to allow growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-early and peremptory reduction of knowledge into arts and methods can arrest growth; while in aphorisms knowledge grows, when fixed in exact methods further substantive increase is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalize only after sufficient exploration; allow fields to develop informally (aphorisms, observations) before imposing rigid methods that may freeze progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain universality (philosophia prima) to enable deeper discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: After distribution into particular arts, abandonment of universality prevents perfect discovery; one cannot discover remote parts of a science while standing only at its level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and pursue higher, universal principles to enable breakthroughs and access deeper aspects of particular sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize observation of nature over mere intellectualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive adoration of the mind has withdrawn men from contemplation of nature, causing delusion; true philosophers should read in 'the volume of God’s works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance reason with observation; avoid constructing systems purely by internal speculation without testing against experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tinting all inquiry by a preferred art or conceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars often infect their opinions with conceits from arts they most admire, giving all things a tincture according to those arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of disciplinary bias (e.g., Plato's theological tint, Aristotle's logicizing, alchemists' furnace-based philosophy); evaluate topics on their own terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice patient doubt and avoid haste to assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: An impatience of doubt and haste to assert without mature suspension undermines reliable knowledge; beginning with doubts leads to certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspend judgement appropriately; cultivate a methodical patience that allows assertions only after sufficient testing and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present knowledge ingenuously and proportionally to conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition and delivery of knowledge is too often magistral and peremptory rather than ingenuous and faithful; propositions should be made 'sincerely with more or less asseveration' as one’s conviction varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid peremptory teaching that discourages examination; indicate degrees of certainty and allow examination rather than commanding belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim scholarship at adding substantive knowledge, not merely reputation or commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Many convert labour to 'second prizes' like being a profound interpreter, commentator, or abridger, which may improve patrimony but seldom augment science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage original additions to science rather than prioritizing reputation, commentary, or rhetorical victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite contemplation and action; orient learning to practical benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge should not be merely for pleasure or profit but 'as a spouse, for generation, fruit, and comfort'—a conjunction of contemplation (Saturn) and action (Jupiter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek applications of knowledge that relieve human estate and produce lasting fruit; avoid treating learning only as ornament or shop for lucre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learning to exalt divine glory and guard against unbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal duties of human learning relative to faith: to exalt the glory of God and to serve as a preservative against unbelief by studying Scripture and creatures together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study both the Scriptures (revealing God's will) and creatures (expressing His power); natural knowledge aids theological understanding and belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value practical inventions and arts as high human merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients consecrated inventors and authors of new arts among the gods because their merits are permanent and universal compared to purely civil or temporal merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor and encourage invention and contributions to the arts and useful technologies that have enduring, universal benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage learned rulers and governors
rubrics_metrics.description: Times under learned princes and governors have been the best; learned governors proceed on safer and more substantial principles than mere men of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote education among rulers and counsellors: learned leadership better averts ruinous errors and preserves social felicity.
